reading.body:
CyrusOne's Sterling NVA9 carries 38 MW of IT load across 700,000 square feet, about 2.4 percent of the 1,603 MW disclosed by Virginia's reporting data centers.

Disclosure is the exception in Virginia, not the rule. The state has 330 mapped data center facilities and only 25 publish a capacity figure. That 1,603 MW total is therefore a floor on installed IT load, not a census. Sterling ranks 13th within that disclosed subset, which makes it mid-scale among the facilities that state anything at all.

For AI workloads the number that matters is power per rack, and none is published here. At an assumed 40 kW per rack, 38 MW supports roughly 950 racks. That is an assumption about possible scale rather than a specification. A lower density would fit more racks on the same power while delivering less AI compute, so the rack count alone does not settle what the building can train.

What the data does not cover is as important as what it does. No certifications are listed, so nothing here establishes which workload classes the facility is qualified to host. No grid capacity or interconnection figure appears, so nothing here establishes whether the surrounding power system can absorb additional load. Announced expansion is absent too, and the suitability score of 69 names it as the missing input, resting only on published IT capacity and operator type.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
